current_activity: Leading units disembark in France; the corps has no operational responsibilities for the moment
notes: Event date: 7 July 1944 (Stacey, p. 152). Event definition: The leading units of the division disembark in France; for the moment Simonds corps, whose main headquarters opened at Camilly a week after 29 June, has no operational responsibilities (p. 152). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 152: "The 2nd Canadian Infantry Division was also on the move to France; its leading units disembarked on 7 July". Location: Juno Beach area (existing area place PL0180) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the existing Juno Beach area place, used as a representative point for the beachhead where Canadian formations landed; it is not a documented landing place. Location support: Stacey gives the date but not the landing place on the pages read. Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Operation Atlantic: 4th Brigade attacks Louvigny west of the Orne; first day in action since Dieppe
notes: Event date: 18 July 1944 (Stacey, pp. 171-172). Event definition: The division fights its first day in action since Dieppe: the 4th Brigade attacks Louvigny, west of the Orne near the mouth of the Odon, in the early evening and The Royal Regiment of Canada clears the orchards north of the village by nightfall; the capture is completed on the morning of 19 July (p. 174). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 171: "The 4th had the particular task of capturing Louvigny, on the Orne near the mouth of the Odon"; p. 172: "Major-General Foulkes' 2nd Canadian Infantry Division was having its first day in action since Dieppe"; p. 174: "The Royal Regiment of Canada had completed the capture of Louvigny on the morning of the 19th". Location: Louvigny, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Louvigny as the objective of the 4th Brigade (p. 171). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Operation Atlantic: 6th Brigade attacks Verrieres Ridge and St. Andre-sur-Orne at 15:00 and is thrown back
notes: Event date: 20 July 1944, 15:00 (Stacey, pp. 174-175). Event definition: The 6th Brigade attacks the Verrieres Ridge, the Camerons on St. Andre-sur-Orne, the South Saskatchewan Regiment on the middle of the ridge and Les Fusiliers Mont-Royal on Verrieres; the Camerons keep a foothold in St. Andre and the Fusiliers take Beauvoir and Troteval Farms, but the South Saskatchewan Regiment suffer a bloody reverse after 17:32 (p. 175). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 174: "On the morning of 20 July the 6th Brigade was moving south across the Orne preparatory to attacking this feature"; p. 175: "Les Fusiliers Mont-Royal on the. left had as their objective Verrieres"; "The South Saskatchewan Regiment, after overcoming considerable opposition, reported two companies on their objectives, at 5:32 p.m.". Location: Verrieres Ridge, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names the ridge and Verrieres as the objective of the 6th Brigade (pp. 174-175). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Operation Spring: division attacks May-sur-Orne and Verrieres on the right of the corps front at 03:30
notes: Event date: 25 July 1944, 03:30 (Stacey, p. 186). Event definition: The first phase of Operation Spring falls on the right to the 2nd Division, which is to attack May-sur-Orne and Verrieres while on the left the 3rd Division captures Tilly-la-Campagne; D Day is confirmed as 25 July and H Hour as 03:30 (p. 186). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 186: "D Day was confirmed as 25 July and H Hour as 3:30 a.m."; "The first phase, on the right, would be the business of the 2nd Canadian Infantry Division". Location: Verrieres Ridge, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names May-sur-Orne and Verrieres as the objectives of the division (p. 186). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Totalize phase II: Royal Regiment takes Gaumesnil at 15:30; Calgary Highlanders and Maisonneuve take Bretteville
notes: Event date: 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 224). Event definition: In the second phase of Operation Totalize The Royal Regiment of Canada captures Gaumesnil at 15:30 and the 2nd Division attacks Bretteville-sur-Laize at 16:00, The Calgary Highlanders and Le Regiment de Maisonneuve taking the village; the Calgary Highlanders then withdraw to the higher ground north of it with heavy losses. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 224: "farther to the right, the 2nd Division attacked"; "The Calgary Highlanders and Le Regiment de Maisonneuve attacked supported by the 1st Hussars, and the village was duly taken"; "captured the village at 3:30 p.m.". Location: Bretteville-sur-Laize, Calvados (existing place PL0525) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Bretteville-sur-Laize and Gaumesnil (p. 224). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: 6th Brigade attacks Falaise at 15:00 with South Saskatchewan and Camerons; Ecole Superieure held out
notes: Event date: 16 August 1944, 15:00 (Stacey, p. 250). Event definition: The task of taking Falaise falls to the 2nd Division: the 6th Brigade attacks the town at 15:00 with The South Saskatchewan Regiment on the left and The Cameron Highlanders of Canada on the right; by the morning of 17 August the South Saskatchewans are on the railway east of the town. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 250: "The task of taking the tragic ruins"; "Brigadier Young was ordered to clear the town with the 6th Brigade, and attacked at 3:00 p.m.". Location: Falaise, Calvados with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names the town of Falaise as the objective (p. 250). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Last resistance in Falaise ends about 02:00 when the Fusiliers Mont-Royal take the Ecole Superieure
notes: Event date: 18 August 1944, about 02:00 (Stacey, p. 250). Event definition: Les Fusiliers Mont-Royal clear fifty or sixty Hitler Youth in the Ecole Superieure in the centre of the town, ending the resistance in Falaise about 02:00 on 18 August; the Camerons had finished their task on 17 August. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 250: "The job of mopping up the last resistance in Falaise, one which was far from easy, was left to Les Fusiliers Mont-Royal"; "Resistance here finally ended only about 2:00 a.m. on 18 August". Location: Falaise, Calvados with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names the Ecole Superieure in the centre of Falaise (p. 250). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: 6th Brigade advances into the Foret de la Londe and meets the German rearguard
notes: Event date: 27 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 291). Event definition: The division fights in the Foret de la Londe south of the Seine bend: on the morning of 27 August the 6th Brigade advances along the road north-east from Bourgtheroulde, the Camerons moving east towards Moulineaux into strong opposition including tanks and Les Fusiliers Mont-Royal into the enemy at Le Buquet; (pp. 290-291). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 291: "On the morning of the 27th the brigade advanced along the road running north-east from Bourgtheroulde"; p. 290: "At 4:00 p.m. General Foulkes held an orders group". Location: Foret de la Londe, Seine-Maritime with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the forest centre; the fighting took place along its length. Location support: Stacey names the forest, Bourgtheroulde, Moulineaux and Le Buquet (pp. 290-291). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Returns to Dieppe unopposed after the Germans leave; Operation Fusilade cancelled
notes: Event date: 1 September 1944 (Stacey, p. 300). Event definition: The division returns to Dieppe, where it fought the raid of 19 August 1942: the 8th Reconnaissance Regiment reaches the outskirts early on 1 September and finds that the German rear parties left the day before, so that the Bomber Command attack of Operation Fusilade is cancelled with twenty minutes to spare; the main bodies reach the town during the day. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 300: "On 1 September the 2nd Canadian Infantry Division returned to Dieppe"; "In the course of the day the main bodies of the 2nd Division reached the town". Location: Dieppe, Seine-Maritime with a precision of 5 km. Location support: Stacey names Dieppe (p. 300). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Begins moving to the Antwerp area and relieves the 53rd Division; enemy holds the northern outskirts
notes: Event date: 16 September 1944 (Stacey, p. 365). Event definition: From 16 September the division moves to the Antwerp area and relieves the 53rd (Welsh) Division; when the 4th Brigade moves into Antwerp the enemy still holds the northern outskirts and the harbour locks are under German artillery fire. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 365: "beginning on 16 September, the 2nd Canadian Infantry Division moved to the Antwerp area, where it relieved the 53rd (Welsh) Division". Location: Antwerp, Belgium (existing place PL0574) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: Stacey says the Antwerp area; the point is the city and the movement lasted several days from 16 September. Location support: Stacey names the Antwerp area (p. 365). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Placed temporarily under I Corps; to pass through the 49th Division bridgehead on the Antwerp-Turnhout canal
notes: Event date: 26 September 1944 (Stacey, p. 367). Event definition: The division is placed temporarily under I Corps (Stacey: 1st British Corps) to reduce the front of II Canadian Corps; after failing to cross the Antwerp-Turnhout Canal in the Lochtenberg area it is to pass through the bridgehead of the 49th Division, the 5th Brigade going into action there on 28 September. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 367: "On the 26th the 2nd Canadian Corps' front was reduced by placing the 2nd Canadian Division temporarily under the 1st British Corps"; "the decision was taken to pass it through the bridgehead already established by the 49th Division". Location: Antwerp, Belgium (existing place PL0574) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the canal crossing lies several miles north-east of the city; the point is the city, with a wide precision. Location support: Stacey names the Antwerp area and the Antwerp-Turnhout Canal (p. 367). Commander: Maj.-Gen. C. Foulkes (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: 11 Jan. 44 to 9 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Passes back from I Corps to II Canadian Corps at midnight 6-7 October, less than three miles from Woensdrecht
notes: Event date: 7 October 1944, midnight of 6-7 October (Stacey, p. 381). Event definition: After Ossendrecht and Santvliet are taken on 6 October, with Woensdrecht less than three miles away, the division passes from I Corps back to II Canadian Corps at midnight of 6-7 October; the divisional plan is to pass the 5th Brigade through the 4th and push up the main road directed on Korteven, beyond Woensdrecht, on 7 October (p. 382); Brigadier Keefler commands the division while Foulkes commands the corps (p. 373). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 381: "On the 6th Ossendrecht and Santvliet were taken, and with Woensdrecht less than three miles away"; "at midnight of 6-7 October, the 2nd Division passed from the 1st British to the 2nd Canadian Corps". Location: Woensdrecht, Noord-Brabant with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the front lay a little south of the village (Ossendrecht); the point is the objective village. Location support: Stacey names Woensdrecht as the next objective, less than three miles from the front on 6 October (p. 381). Commander: Brig. R. H. Keefler commanded the division while Foulkes commanded the corps (Stacey, p. 373).

current_activity: Royal Hamilton Light Infantry attack the Woensdrecht feature at 03:30 behind a heavy barrage with tanks
notes: Event date: 16 October 1944, 03:30 (Stacey, p. 384). Event definition: The 4th Brigade attacks the Woensdrecht feature: The Royal Hamilton Light Infantry advance at 03:30 behind a heavy barrage with the tanks of the 10th Armoured Regiment; the feature is not completely controlled and the enemy infiltrates (p. 385), but on 16 October the German command in the west records that a permanent recapture of the land connection with Walcheren can no longer be expected (p. 386). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 384: "did not take place until 16 October"; "At 3:30 a.m. that day The Royal Hamilton Light Infantry put it in". Location: Woensdrecht, Noord-Brabant with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Woensdrecht as the objective (p. 384). Commander: Brig. R. H. Keefler commanded the division while Foulkes commanded the corps (Stacey, p. 373).

current_activity: Maisonneuve attack across the Walcheren causeway at 04:00, to be relieved at 05:00 by the Lowland Division
notes: Event date: 2 November 1944, 04:00 (Stacey, pp. 404-405). Event definition: After the Canadian Black Watch attempt of 31 October is withdrawn that evening and The Calgary Highlanders renew the attack, Le Regiment de Maisonneuve is to attack across the Walcheren causeway with heavy artillery support at 04:00 on 2 November to re-establish the bridgehead, and is to be relieved at 05:00 by the Glasgow Highlanders, the leading unit of the 157th Brigade of the Lowland Division (p. 405). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 404: "The first attempt was made early in the afternoon of 31 October by the Canadian Black Watch with one company"; p. 405: "the Maisonneuves should attack across the causeway with heavy artillery support at 4:00 a.m. on 2 November and re-establish the bridgehead on Walcheren". Location: Sloedam (Walcheren causeway), Zeeland with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: Stacey says the causeway across the flooded isthmus; the point is the Sloedam at its centre. Location support: Stacey names the causeway to Walcheren and the brigade tactical headquarters about a mile south-east of its eastern end (p. 404). Commander: Brig. R. H. Keefler commanded the division while Foulkes commanded the corps (Stacey, p. 373).

current_activity: Takes the right of the corps front opposite the Reichswald between Cuijk and Groesbeek; Matthews commands
notes: Event date: 10 November 1944 (Stacey, p. 430; Appendix G). Event definition: In the Nijmegen sector taken over from the British 30th Corps the division holds the right of the corps front opposite the Reichswald, between Cuijk and Groesbeek; Maj.-Gen. A. B. Matthews takes the division on 10 November (Appendix G). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 428: "The 2nd Canadian Corps was directed to take over the Nijmegen sector from the 30th British Corps"; p. 430: "the 2nd Canadian opposite the Reichswald, between Cuijk and Groesbeek". Location: Groesbeek, Gelderland with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the front runs from Cuijk to Groesbeek; the point is Groesbeek and stands for the sector, with a wide precision. Location support: Stacey names the sector between Cuijk and Groesbeek (p. 430). Commander: Maj.-Gen. A. B. Matthews (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: from 10 Nov. 44).

current_activity: Black Watch company raid near Knapheide south of Groesbeek: about 25 Germans killed, one prisoner
notes: Event date: 7 December 1944 (Stacey, p. 435). Event definition: A well organised company raid by The Black Watch (Royal Highland Regiment) of Canada near Knapheide, south of Groesbeek, one of many raids and patrols of the winter on the Nijmegen front; the enemy is thought to lose about 25 killed and one prisoner is taken, the Black Watch having nine fatal casualties. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 435: "carried out near Knapheide, south of Groesbeek, on 7 December by The Black Watch (Royal Highland Regiment) of Canada"; "In this company raid it was estimated that the enemy lost about 25 killed, while one prisoner was taken". Location: Groesbeek, Gelderland with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: Knapheide is a hamlet south of Groesbeek; the point is Groesbeek. Location support: Stacey names Knapheide, south of Groesbeek (p. 435). Commander: Maj.-Gen. A. B. Matthews (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 665: from 10 Nov. 44).
